extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in creative nonfiction film (filmmakers, critics, workshop participants)
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing feature-length or special-format films (hybrid/experimental documentaries) to determine if and how they function as creative nonfiction, focusing on formal choices, self-reflexivity, and emotional truth rather than purely factual accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creative nonfiction as subjective translation of reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Creative nonfiction describes documentaries that push the boundaries of what we traditionally consider documentary to be — the best nonfiction 'translates reality for the audience rather than presenting it plainly and objectively.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the film is aiming to convey an emotional or subjective experience rather than a literal chronicle of events; the piece's value can lie in how it renders internal states, not in strict factual reportage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visibility of the filmmaking process / showing production apparatus
rubrics_metrics.description: Making the process visible on screen (showing camera, lighting tests, equipment, editing moments) so viewers are aware someone is making choices about what they see.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Burnham's lighting and camera tests at the film's start; Kirsten Johnson's Dick Johnson is Dead showing camera equipment and voiceover recording. This technique 'reminds us that someone is making choices' and encourages critical viewing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternation between staged performance and vérité/candid footage
rubrics_metrics.description: Constantly alternating highly produced musical/performance numbers with verite-style, 'behind-the-scenes' or candid footage to create contrast and delineate performer vs. 'real' person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how the cuts between produced and candid material function: do they reveal tension between persona and private self? Example: cutting from an elaborate number to Burnham slumped watching it on his laptop.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-reflexivity and meta-commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: The artist observes, re-watches, or comments on their own work within the piece (meta acts that flag self-awareness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for scenes where the filmmaker watches/edits/reviews their own footage, or otherwise calls attention to the constructed nature of the piece; these moments signal reflexive intent rather than simple performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional/psychological truth over literal factual accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritising the representation of an emotional experience (e.g., 'the emotional rollercoaster of a year of lockdown') even if the literal facts are simplified, omitted, or altered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticisms about factual omissions (e.g., Burnham's partner, living arrangements) can be weighed against whether the film successfully communicates the felt experience of quarantine; psychological plausibility can justify departures from literal accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal/visual language mapping to internal arc
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of changing visual style, editing, and camera movement to reflect the subject's emotional progression (e.g., pristine/precise to abstract/messy; multi-cut numbers to single-take; camera picked up and moved wildly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess coherence between formal choices and narrative/psychological arc: do mise-en-scène, shot construction, and editing evolve to mirror the subject's mental state (e.g., increasing abstraction as depression deepens)?

rubrics_metrics.name: Character arc as organizing principle rather than set-piece quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluating individual set pieces primarily for what they reveal about the creator's character arc (motivation, mental state, development) instead of judging them only on entertainment/comedic success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: 'What does this piece say about the character of the filmmaker that he chose to make it now?' — this reframes assessment from 'is it funny?' to 'what does it reveal?'

rubrics_metrics.name: Reuse of derivative material as intentional signal
rubrics_metrics.description: Rehashing earlier bits or tired observations can be purposeful: early derivative sketches show a character leaning on 'tried and tested modes of humour' when lost or high-energy at the start.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't treat derivation as automatic failure; consider whether repetition functions narratively (e.g., to indicate creative stagnation, dependence on old modes, or a phase in the subject's arc).

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance of authenticity — candid footage is still performative
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledgement that both staged performances and 'candid' behind-the-scenes moments involve degrees of performance; the film's authenticity is a crafted effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how performativity is used: is the performance in service of accessing an emotional truth? Consider whether 'candid' moments are presented and framed to achieve a particular emotional response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of confined/symbolic space as psychological metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: Employing a single, contained setting (e.g., one white room) as a visually translated psychological space that conveys claustrophobia, isolation, or other internal states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the setting functions metaphorically to embody the subject's interior life; the literal implausibility (e.g., living arrangements) can be acceptable if the space effectively externalises the emotional tenor.
